activities.prompt:
Explain to a friend who knows Lua why print("3" + "4") shows 34 in Python, while print(3 + "4") stops with an error.

Input requirement: keyboard text entry for the explanation. Read the supplied model and self-check; prose is not automatically graded. A remote alone is insufficient.
activities.explanation: "3" and "4" are both strings, so + joins them into "34". In 3 + "4", one side is a number and the other a string. Python refuses to guess, so it raises a TypeError. Lua would coerce "4" to a number here; in Python you write int("4") or str(3) yourself.

activities.prompt:
Explain to a Lua programmer why if 0: skips its block in Python, even though if 0 then runs its block in Lua. When would that difference bite you?

Input requirement: keyboard text entry for the explanation. Read the supplied model and self-check; prose is not automatically graded. A remote alone is insufficient.
activities.explanation: Python treats zero, empty strings, empty collections and None as false, so if 0: skips. Lua treats only nil and false as false, so 0 is true there. It bites when a value can legitimately be 0, like a score: if score: would skip a real score of 0. Say what you mean, e.g. if score is not None.

activities.prompt:
Explain to a friend: what is a base case, what happens without one (or if calls never reach it), and how the call stack lets fact(3) work out 3 × 2 × 1 when no single call knows the whole answer.

Input requirement: keyboard text entry for the explanation. Read the supplied model and self-check; prose is not automatically graded. A remote alone is insufficient.
activities.explanation: A base case is the smallest version of the problem, answered directly (fact(1) is 1). Without one, or if each call doesn't get closer to it, the function keeps calling itself until Python runs out of stack and raises a RecursionError. fact(3) can't finish until fact(2) does, which waits on fact(1). Each waiting call keeps its own n in its own box on the call stack. fact(1) answers 1, then fact(2) finishes 2 × 1, then fact(3) finishes 3 × 2. The newest box always finishes first.
